summary.text: Ocean currents are continuous, directed flows of seawater driven by forces including wind, the Coriolis effect, and differences in temperature and salinity.
Surface currents are generally driven by wind, while deep-water currents are driven by differences in water density caused by temperature and salinity.
Together the currents form a global conveyor belt that carries heat around the globe and has a large impact on Earth's climate.

items.prompt: Northwest Europe is much milder than other places at the same high latitude. What mainly explains this?

options.label: Its many mountains block Arctic winds
It receives more sunlight than those places
Warm water carried by the Gulf Stream

items.explain: The Gulf Stream and its extension, the North Atlantic Drift, make northwest Europe much more temperate than other areas at its latitude.

items.prompt: Lima, Peru, sits at a tropical latitude yet has a cooler climate than its surroundings. What is the cause?

options.label: Its great distance from the sea
Winds blowing in from the Amazon

items.explain: Lima's cooler subtropical climate contrasts with the surrounding tropics because of the Humboldt Current.

items.prompt: Deep currents begin where surface water becomes dense enough to sink. Which two properties together set seawater's density?
items.explain: Thermohaline refers to temperature and salt content, the factors that together determine seawater's density.

items.prompt: Water that sinks in the North Atlantic travels through the deep ocean before rising again. Roughly how long have the oldest waters been travelling when they rise in the North Pacific?
items.explain: The oldest waters, with a transit time of around 1000 years, upwell in the North Pacific.

items.prompt: A steady wind blows across the open ocean. Which way does the surface current it drives flow?

options.label: At an angle to the wind

items.explain: Because of the Ekman spiral, wind-driven currents flow at an angle to the winds that drive them.

items.prompt: Why do vertical currents, where water rises or sinks, matter beyond just moving water?

options.label: They carry nutrients and gases between deep and surface
They create the tides along coastlines
They make the sea saltier over time
They set the direction the wind blows

items.explain: Upwelling and downwelling play an important role in moving nutrients and gases, such as carbon dioxide, between the surface and the deep ocean.

beats.title: Rivers Inside the Sea
beats.hook: Northwest Europe owes its mild weather to water that set out from the equatorial Atlantic.

beats.prompt: Match each kind of moving water to its description

right.label: Larger masses of water, faster than either
More definite direction, faster than a drift
Surface water pushed forward by the prevailing wind

beats.explain: Moving seawater is classed by velocity, size and direction, from slow wind-pushed drifts up to large, fast streams like the Gulf Stream.

beats.prompt: Put these steps of the Atlantic conveyor in order

items.label: Surface water travels polewards from the equatorial Atlantic
It sinks at high latitudes as North Atlantic Deep Water
The dense water flows on into the ocean basins

beats.explain: Wind-driven surface water heads polewards, cools en route, sinks at high latitudes, and then spreads as dense water into the ocean basins.

beats.prompt: Suppose the current bringing warm water up the north Atlantic to northwest Europe stopped. What would you expect along those coasts?
beats.explain: That warm current slowly keeps ice from forming along the seashores, ice that would otherwise block ships from seaports and inland waterways.

choices.label: Nothing would change, since air alone sets climate
choices.feedback: Ocean currents strongly influence the temperature of the regions they pass through.

choices.label: Coasts would warm as the heat stayed put
choices.feedback: The current is what delivers the heat; without it the coasts lose warmth rather than gain it.

choices.label: Ports would dry out as the sea level fell
choices.feedback: The current's role here is heat, not the height of the sea.

choices.label: Ice could form along shores and block ships

beats.prompt: One step in this reasoning is wrong; which?

steps.text: Surface currents are generally driven by wind systems.
Deep-water currents are driven by differences in water density.
Seawater density depends on its temperature and salt content.
So deep currents can only start where the wind blows hardest.

beats.explain: Deep circulation is driven by density gradients created by surface heat and freshwater fluxes, not by where the wind is strongest.

beats.idea: Wind pushes surface currents and density differences drive deep ones, and together they carry heat around the globe, shaping the climate of whole regions.

paragraphs.heading: Rivers in the sea
paragraphs.text: An ocean current is a steady, directed flow of seawater. Forces such as wind, breaking waves, and differences in temperature and salinity drive it. The shape of the sea floor and coastline, along with other currents, steer its direction and strength. Currents are measured in sverdrups (Sv), where 1 Sv is a flow of 1,000,000 m³ of water every second.

paragraphs.heading: Surface and deep
paragraphs.text: There are two main kinds: surface currents and deep-water currents. Surface currents are mostly driven by wind; big prevailing winds drive major lasting currents, while seasonal or occasional winds drive currents that last about as long as those winds do. Deep-water currents are driven by differences in density, which come from changes in temperature and salinity. Currents flow sideways across whole oceans and also up and down, and this upwelling and downwelling carries nutrients and gases, carbon dioxide among them, between the surface and the deep.

paragraphs.heading: The global conveyor belt
paragraphs.text: The density-driven part is called the thermohaline circulation: "thermo" refers to temperature and "haline" to salt, which together set seawater's density. It is also known as the global conveyor belt. Surface currents such as the Gulf Stream travel from the equatorial Atlantic toward the poles, cool on the way, and sink at high latitudes to form North Atlantic Deep Water. This dense water spreads into the ocean basins; most of it rises again in the Southern Ocean, but the oldest water, around 1000 years in transit, comes up in the North Pacific.

paragraphs.heading: Moving heat around the world
paragraphs.text: On their way, these water masses carry heat and matter, including dissolved substances and gases, around the planet, so the state of the circulation strongly affects Earth's climate. Currents change the temperature of the regions they pass. Warm currents along temperate coasts heat the sea breezes blowing over them. The Gulf Stream and its extension, the North Atlantic Drift, make northwest Europe much milder than other places at the same high latitude, while the Humboldt Current gives Lima, Peru, a cooler climate than the tropics around it.

paragraphs.heading: Drifts, currents and streams
paragraphs.text: Currents are sorted by temperature into warm and cold ones, and by speed, size and direction into drifts, currents and streams. Drifts, like the North Atlantic Drift, are surface water pushed forward by the prevailing wind. Currents, like the Labrador Current, move faster than drifts and in a clearer direction. Streams, like the Gulf Stream, move larger masses of water faster still.

paragraphs.heading: The biggest current
paragraphs.text: The largest current of all is the Antarctic Circumpolar Current, a wind-driven flow that circles Antarctica clockwise without a break. It links all the ocean basins, and water rising and sinking on either side of it connects the atmosphere to the deep ocean. Since the 2000s, an international program called Argo has used a fleet of automated floats drifting with the currents to map the ocean's temperature and salinity. What it gathers will help explain the ocean's role in Earth's climate.
